title: feat(hooks): one dispatcher process per claude event, rules run in-process
description:
## .what

register ONE hook command per claude event (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit), which loads every enrolled role's hook rules once and runs them **in-process**. today `rhx init --hooks` writes one command per rule, so every tool call starts one process per rule.

## .why — measured on a laptop with ~10 busy claude sessions

one Bash tool call fires 10 PreToolUse hooks: 3 `rhx … --mode hook` (bhrain driver + learner) and 7 `bash …/pretooluse.*.sh` (ehmpathy mechanic). cpu = user+sys of each hook's process tree via `/usr/bin/time`, median of 3–5 runs, a benign `pwd` call:

| shape | cpu per Bash call | peak rss |
|---|---|---|
| today: 10 separate hook processes | **2010–2110 ms** (startup ~1190, the rules' own work ~900) | 207 MB at once |
| one dispatcher that spawns 10 rhx children (serial or parallel, same cpu) | ~3130 ms, startup alone | 53 MB each |
| **one dispatcher, rules in-process** | **~1200 ms** est. (one boot 280 + work) | **52 MB** |

- floor: one rhx boot with no work = 280 ms cpu, 52 MB; one bash hook with no work = 40–50 ms, 7 MB
- at ~2 Bash calls/sec across sessions, the hooks burn ~4 cpu-seconds per second: ~4 of 12 cores, around the clock
- the in-process estimate is a floor on the gain: most of each rhx hook's "work" (110–270 ms) is that process's own load of its role code, which one process does once; the checks themselves are regexes
- a dispatcher that spawns children is WORSE than today; only the in-process fan-out wins

## .shape

- `rhx init --hooks` writes one entry per event, e.g. `rhx hooks.dispatch --event PreToolUse`, whose matcher is the union of all rules' matchers
- the dispatcher reads stdin once, parses once, runs each rule whose matcher fits the tool, and exits 2 at the first block with that rule's message (or aggregates all blocks — a choice to make)
- shell-authored rules (the mechanic `pretooluse.*.sh`) need an in-process path too: a TS port, or a declared pure-pattern form, so most never need a shell
- one timeout per rule inside the dispatcher, so one slow rule cannot eat the event budget

## .done bar

- a Bash tool call starts 1 hook process, not 10
- `rhx claude.hooks.cost --tool Bash` (uladkasach/dev-env-setup) shows ≤ ~1200 ms cpu and ≤ ~55 MB per call, down from ~2010 ms / 207 MB

## .stacked

a follow-up task adds an `onTool` regex filter per rule, which lets this dispatcher skip its own boot on a call no rule wants. it builds on this task.
